title: Emergence from the Panther Splits
body:
The Black Liberation Army emerged around 1970–1971 as an underground armed formation, growing out of the crisis that FBI repression and internal conflict had produced within the Black Panther Party. As the March 1971 split between Huey Newton's Oakland-based leadership and Eldridge Cleaver's international faction tore the party apart, members who believed the moment called for clandestine armed struggle went underground.

Unlike the Panthers' public organization, the BLA had no formal above-ground structure; it operated as a decentralized network of cells drawn from Panther veterans and other Black revolutionaries. Its stated aim was to take up arms for the liberation and self-determination of Black people in the United States, and its members saw themselves as combatants in a war against a repressive state.

title: Killing of NYPD Officers Piagentini & Jones
body:
On May 21, 1971, New York City police officers Joseph Piagentini and Waverly Jones were shot and killed in Harlem in an ambush attributed to the Black Liberation Army. Coming amid a wave of attacks on police, the killings drew intense law-enforcement attention to the emerging underground.

Years of investigation and prosecution followed. Herman Bell, Jalil Muntaqim (Anthony Bottom), and Albert "Nuh" Washington — the "New York Three" — were convicted in the case and became long-term political prisoners. Their decades-long imprisonment, and the campaigns for their release, made the case one of the most enduring in the history of BLA-related prosecutions; Bell and Muntaqim were finally paroled only in 2018.

title: Killing of NYPD Officers Foster & Laurie
body:
On January 27, 1972, New York City police officers Gregory Foster and Rocco Laurie were shot and killed on the Lower East Side, another killing attributed to Black Liberation Army militants. Coming eight months after the Piagentini and Jones killings, it intensified the massive police manhunt for the underground network.

The case fed a sweeping federal and local campaign against the BLA and its suspected members, producing arrests, shootouts, and prosecutions across several states. It remains one of the defining episodes cited in accounts of the BLA's armed campaign against the police.

title: Delta Flight 841 Hijacking
body:
On July 31, 1972, a group associated in many accounts with Black liberation militants hijacked Delta Air Lines Flight 841 and, after collecting a $1 million ransom, ordered it flown to Algiers — the largest ransom obtained in a U.S. hijacking to that point.

In Algeria the hijackers initially sought refuge with Eldridge Cleaver's Black Panther International Section, but the Algerian government seized the ransom and returned it to the United States. Several of those involved were later captured in France, tried, and imprisoned there rather than extradited — an episode that tied the American Black liberation underground to the wider currents of 1970s international exile and armed struggle.

title: New Jersey Turnpike Shootout & the Assata Shakur Case
body:
On May 2, 1973, a New Jersey State Police stop on the Turnpike erupted into a shootout that left state trooper Werner Foerster and Black Liberation Army member Zayd Malik Shakur dead. Assata Shakur (JoAnne Chesimard) and Sundiata Acoli were wounded and captured.

Assata Shakur — already the target of a series of prosecutions, most of which had ended in acquittals or dismissals — was convicted of Foerster's murder in 1977 in a case her supporters have long argued was deeply flawed, noting medical evidence that she could not have fired a weapon. Sundiata Acoli was also convicted and would spend nearly half a century in prison before his 2022 parole. The case became one of the central and most contested in the BLA's history.

title: Assata Shakur’s Prison Escape
body:
On November 2, 1979, Assata Shakur escaped from the Clinton Correctional Facility for Women in New Jersey with the help of armed comrades linked to the Black Liberation Army and the May 19th Communist Organization, who entered the prison and spirited her away without a shot fired.

After years underground she surfaced in Cuba, which granted her political asylum in 1984; she has lived there ever since. Her escape and exile made her an enduring symbol of the era's Black liberation struggle — and a lasting object of official pursuit, as the U.S. government placed her on its Most Wanted Terrorists list in 2013 and repeatedly demanded her return.

title: The 1981 Brink’s Robbery
body:
On October 20, 1981, a coalition of Black Liberation Army members and white radicals from the May 19th Communist Organization robbed a Brink's armored truck at the Nanuet Mall in Rockland County, New York. The robbery went catastrophically wrong: Brink's guard Peter Paige was killed at the mall, and moments later, at a roadblock in nearby Nyack, police officers Edward O'Grady and Waverly Brown — the latter the town's first Black officer — were shot and killed.

The failed robbery led to a sweeping federal investigation and prosecutions that effectively dismantled what remained of the armed underground. Defendants including Kuwasi Balagoon, Sekou Odinga, Mutulu Shakur, and the Weather Underground veteran David Gilbert drew long sentences; several, along with Marilyn Buck, became prominent long-term political prisoners.

title: Mutulu Shakur Prosecution
body:
Mutulu Shakur — an acupuncturist and Black liberation activist, and stepfather of Tupac Shakur — was prosecuted in federal court in the 1980s for his role in the 1981 Brink's robbery and a broader pattern of underground activity, including the 1979 prison escape of Assata Shakur. Captured in 1986 after years as a fugitive, he was convicted under federal racketeering (RICO) statutes.

Sentenced to sixty years, Shakur became one of the most prominent BLA-linked political prisoners, and his repeated, long-denied bids for parole drew wide support. He was finally released on compassionate grounds in December 2022, gravely ill with cancer, and died in July 2023 — his case a touchstone for campaigns against the indefinite imprisonment of aging political prisoners.

title: Long-Term Political-Prisoner Campaigns
body:
From the 1980s onward, the men and women imprisoned in connection with the Black Liberation Army became central figures in U.S. political-prisoner organizing. Because they received exceptionally long sentences and were repeatedly denied parole, BLA prisoners — among them Herman Bell, Jalil Muntaqim, Sundiata Acoli, Mutulu Shakur, Sekou Odinga, and Russell Maroon Shoatz — came to represent the enduring afterlife of the Black liberation movement inside the prison system.

Decades-long campaigns organized around their cases, framing them as prisoners of a domestic war and linking their fate to the exposure of COINTELPRO and the broader history of state repression. Over time several were paroled, released, or died in or shortly after custody, but their long imprisonments remain among the most cited examples of political incarceration in the United States.
